## Role and Scope

The balance of plant (BOP) includes the non-electrical auxiliary equipment required to operate the PEM electrolyser stack safely and continuously. In this model, the BOP manages feedwater supply, heat removal, gas-liquid separation, hydrogen drying, hydrogen-side piping, instrumentation and housing.

Because the system is offshore, the feedwater system must also include seawater intake, desalination and final purification to electrolyser-grade water.

Power electronics are excluded completely because the required components depend on the electrical architecture. Transformers, rectifiers and other electrical conversion equipment are discussed on [Electrolyser Power Electronics](elx_power_electronics.qmd).

The stack, compressors, hydrogen export system, offshore installation, offshore structures and indirect project costs are also represented elsewhere in the model.

The scope used in this page is therefore:

| Included in this BOP model          | Excluded from this BOP model        |
| ----------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| Thermal management                  | PEM electrolyser stack              |
| Feedwater handling                  | Power electronics                   |
| Seawater intake                     | Transformers and rectifiers         |
| Desalination and final purification | Hydrogen compression                |
| Gas-liquid separation               | Hydrogen export system              |
| Hydrogen drying                     | Offshore foundations and structures |
| Hydrogen-side BOP piping            | Offshore installation               |
| Instrumentation and housing         | Site preparation and indirect costs |

: Scope boundary for the balance-of-plant model.

## Key Assumptions

The main assumptions used in the base-case BOP model are:

| Parameter                                   |      Base value | Comment                                              |
| ------------------------------------------- | --------------: | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| Non-water non-electrical BOP reference cost | 333 2020 USD/kW | NREL 1,000 MW/year case plus 50% manufacturer markup |
| Water-treatment reference purchase cost (1 MW) | {{< var bop-water-reference-purchase-cost >}} | Part of the aggregate BOP; quoted packages are evidence only [@chicoMoreno2021OffshoreElectrolyzer] |
| Reference capacity                          |            1 MW | NREL reference system                                |
| BOP scaling exponent | {{< var bop-scaling-exponent >}} | Applies to the whole BOP, including water treatment |
| Maximum capacity per BOP block | {{< var bop-block-limit >}} | Adopted screening bound, not supplier qualification |
| BOP electricity consumption                 | {{< var bop-specific-electricity >}} H₂ | Excludes compression and power electronics |

: Main base-case assumptions for the BOP model.

These assumptions should be interpreted as early-stage modelling values. The NREL reference system is a land-based 1 MW manufactured-cost estimate. Applying it to offshore multi-MW or GW-scale systems introduces uncertainty because offshore systems require different packaging, redundancy, corrosion protection, maintainability, water intake, cooling strategy and safety zoning. The non-water scaling exponent captures generic economies of scale; water treatment is sized by the peak clean-water flow and discrete treatment packages below.

## Cost Basis

### Scope of Cost Estimate

The non-electrical BOP cost is based on the NREL PEM electrolyser manufactured cost analysis [@badgett2024PEMCost]. NREL reports subsystem costs for a 1 MW PEM electrolyser system in 2020 USD per kW of electrolyser capacity (Table 10).

The base case uses the NREL 1,000 MW/year manufacturing-volume case because the offshore hydrogen system considered here represents industrial-scale deployment rather than early low-volume manufacturing.

Electrical BOP is excluded from the NREL cost breakdown. The NREL water supply category is also separated from the generic BOP cost because offshore seawater treatment requires an explicit desalination and purification model.

This page distinguishes between three cost levels:

| Cost level              | Meaning                                                                                          | Treatment in this model                 |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------- |
| Manufactured cost       | Factory production cost reported by NREL                                                         | Used as the starting point              |
| Equipment purchase cost | Manufactured cost plus manufacturer markup                                                       | Used for the BOP reference cost         |
| Installed offshore cost | Equipment cost plus installation, structures, offshore logistics, contingency and indirect costs | Excluded here and represented elsewhere |

: Cost levels used to interpret the BOP estimate.

### NREL Reference Cost

The remaining non-water, non-electrical BOP manufactured costs used in the base case are:

| Subsystem                              | Manufactured cost [2020 USD/kW] |
| -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------: |
| Thermal management                     |                              61 |
| Hydrogen processing                    |                              88 |
| Hydrogen-side BOP                      |                               4 |
| Piping, instrumentation and housing    |                              69 |
| **Total non-water non-electrical BOP** |                         **222** |

: Non-water non-electrical BOP manufactured costs from the NREL 1,000 MW/year manufacturing-volume case.

A manufacturer markup of **50%** is applied to convert manufactured cost into an approximate equipment purchase cost. The resulting marked-up non-water BOP reference cost is:

$$
c_\mathrm{BOP,ref} = 1.5 \cdot 222 = 333 \ \mathrm{2020\ USD/kW}
$$

For the 1 MW NREL reference system, this corresponds to:

$$
C_\mathrm{BOP,ref} = 333{,}000 \ \mathrm{2020\ USD}
$$

This value excludes power electronics, stack costs, offshore water treatment, installation, offshore structures, site preparation, indirect costs, inflation and offshore-specific cost adders.

### Offshore Water Treatment

The purchased treatment package converts seawater into electrolyser-grade water. A study of an electrolyser integrated with an offshore wind turbine reports vendor quotes for reverse-osmosis packages with a second RO pass, cleaning, electro-deionisation and controls. The study states that these packages deliver water at the required electrolyser quality [@chicoMoreno2021OffshoreElectrolyzer, Table 43]. Its two complete-package references are:

| Package | Clean-water capacity | Quoted investment | Unit cost at quoted capacity |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Small | 100 m³/day = 4.17 m³/h | €0.30 million | €72,000 per (m³/h) |
| Large | 3,800 m³/day = 158.3 m³/h | €3.0 million | €18,900 per (m³/h) |

: Vendor-quoted RO and deionisation package references, reported in a 2021 study [@chicoMoreno2021OffshoreElectrolyzer]. The €/m³/h values divide package price by package output; they are comparison metrics, not continuously scalable unit rates.

The quotes do not establish the costs of seawater intake, intake screening, stack-water recirculation, offshore installation or additional redundancy. These remain separate unresolved costs. The prices are treated as approximately 2021 euros because the study does not specify the quote dates. No additional manufacturer markup is applied to quoted package prices.

The model treats water treatment as part of the **aggregate BOP**. Its reference purchase cost at the 1 MW reference capacity, `bop-water-reference-purchase-cost` ({{< var bop-water-reference-purchase-cost >}}), is added to the non-water reference cost and scaled with the same exponent and block rule (see [Scaling Method](#scaling-method)). The quotes above are evidence for choosing that value, not a separate calculation. They cannot be read off directly: at 10 L of clean water per kg H₂ and about 19.6 kg/h per MW of stack input at the 3 A/cm² rating, a 1 MW reference needs about 0.2 m³/h, far below the smallest quoted package (4.17 m³/h). The water reference cost therefore remains an unresolved input.

### Scaling Method {#scaling-method}

Cooling, gas-liquid separation, drying, piping and instrumentation can be shared across multiple stacks. The BOP therefore does not scale linearly with installed capacity. Water treatment is scaled in the same way, as part of the aggregate BOP.

Because the exact scaling exponent is not known, the model uses the six-tenths rule as a first-order process-equipment scaling approximation. The six-tenths rule is a standard preliminary process-equipment cost-scaling method in which cost scales with capacity using an exponent close to 0.6 [@engineeringLibretextsPurchasedEquipmentCost; @petersTimmerhausWestPlantDesign].

For a BOP unit with capacity $P_i$, the BOP cost, including water treatment, is:

$$
C_{\mathrm{BOP},i} =
\left(C_\mathrm{BOP,ref}+C_\mathrm{water,ref}\right)
\left(
\frac{P_i}{P_\mathrm{ref}}
\right)^{\alpha}
$$

where $P_\mathrm{ref}$ is the NREL reference capacity ({{< var bop-reference-rating >}}), $C_\mathrm{BOP,ref}$ the marked-up, escalated non-water reference cost, $C_\mathrm{water,ref}$ the water-treatment reference purchase cost and $\alpha$ the scaling exponent ({{< var bop-scaling-exponent >}}). The total is $C_{\mathrm{BOP,total}}=\sum_i C_{\mathrm{BOP},i}$.

Each production location is divided into equally loaded BOP blocks:

$$
n_b=\left\lceil\frac{P_{\mathrm{served}}}{P_{\mathrm{block,max}}}\right\rceil,
\qquad P_i=\frac{P_{\mathrm{served}}}{n_b}.
$$

Here $P_{\mathrm{served}}$ is the wind capacity served at that location [kW],
$P_{\mathrm{block,max}}$ is `bop-block-limit` [kW], and $n_b$ is the integer block
count. Stack overplanting does not increase this BOP sizing basis. Centralised
production shares farm power across its blocks; decentralised production sizes
blocks independently at each turbine.

The whole BOP uses `bop-scaling-exponent`. The block limit is an explicit
modelling choice that prevents unlimited centralisation benefits. Lower limits can be evaluated through named scenario overrides.
No spare block is included. The method is implemented in
`model/hydrogen_production/balance_of_plant.py`; its cost result remains
incomplete while the water reference cost is unset.

### Manufacturing Volume Sensitivity

The base case uses the 1,000 MW/year NREL manufacturing-volume case. The 10 MW/year and 100 MW/year NREL cases may be used in sensitivity analysis to represent less mature supply chains or slower industrial scale-up.

After excluding electrical BOP and separating water supply, the non-water BOP sensitivity values are:

| Manufacturing volume | Non-water non-electrical BOP manufactured cost [2020 USD/kW] | With 50% markup [2020 USD/kW] |
| -------------------: | -----------------------------------------------------------: | ----------------------------: |
|           10 MW/year |                                                          296 |                           444 |
|          100 MW/year |                                                          265 |                           398 |
|        1,000 MW/year |                                                          222 |                           333 |

: Manufacturing-volume sensitivity for the non-water non-electrical BOP cost.

The selected manufacturing-volume case changes $C_\mathrm{BOP,ref}$, while the six-tenths rule determines how this reference cost scales with the size of each shared BOP unit.

Water treatment scales with the same exponent as the rest of the BOP. Water quality, redundancy, offshore intake and installation remain additional design and cost uncertainties.

## BOP Power Consumption

The BOP also consumes electricity during electrolyser operation. This consumption is treated separately from stack electricity consumption.

The BOP power consumption represents parasitic loads from auxiliary systems such as pumps, fans, chillers, recirculation blowers, thermal management and hydrogen drying.

Compression is excluded from this value because compression is represented elsewhere in the model. Electrical conversion losses are also explicitly excluded because power electronics are represented separately.

The NREL report cites a generic BOP electricity consumption of 4.2 kWh/kg H₂ (Table 1), but this value includes electrical losses and is therefore not directly applicable to the non-electrical BOP scope used here [@badgett2024PEMCost].

The underlying Ruth and Ahluwalia source [@badgett2024PEMCost] separates BOP losses into electrical, mechanical and hydrogen-related losses. After excluding electrical losses, the remaining BOP consumption is:

| Operating point         | Mechanical [kWh/kg H₂] | Hydrogen [kWh/kg H₂] | Total [kWh/kg H₂] |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------: | -------------------: | ----------------: |
| Rated power, BOL        |                    1.3 |                  0.2 |               1.5 |
| Rated power, EOL        |                    2.3 |                  0.2 |               2.5 |
| Minimum-loss point, BOL |                    0.4 |                  0.1 |               0.5 |
| Minimum-loss point, EOL |                    0.6 |                  0.1 |               0.7 |

: Non-electrical BOP electricity consumption after excluding electrical losses.

A simple lifetime average gives approximately 2.0 kWh/kg H₂ at rated power and 0.6 kWh/kg H₂ at the minimum-loss operating point. The difference is mainly caused by thermal management. At the minimum-loss operating point, the stack operates more efficiently and therefore produces less waste heat. Lower waste heat reduces the cooling duty and associated mechanical power consumption.

In this study, the stack is deliberately oversized so that the electrolyser usually operates closer to the minimum-loss point than to rated stack operation. The model therefore assumes an average non-electrical BOP power consumption of:

$$
e_\mathrm{BOP} = 1.0 \ \mathrm{kWh/kg_{H_2}}
$$

This value includes mechanical BOP loads and hydrogen drying losses. It is selected as a conservative average. It is higher than the minimum-loss values reported by Ruth and Ahluwalia to allow for offshore cooling, water handling, drying, control systems, part-load operation and uncertainty in auxiliary loads.

### Desalination

Offshore desalination and water polishing are small compared with the main BOP parasitic loads. A worst-case reverse-osmosis electricity use of 5.0 kWh/m³ corresponds to approximately 0.05 kWh/kg H₂ when 10 L of water is required per kg H₂. This is small relative to the assumed 1.0 kWh/kg H₂ BOP consumption.

Desalination power is therefore included within the BOP power allowance unless a separate water-treatment model is used.

The total BOP electricity consumption is calculated as:

$$
E_\mathrm{BOP} = e_\mathrm{BOP} \cdot m_\mathrm{H_2}
$$

where $E_\mathrm{BOP}$ is the BOP electricity consumption and $m_\mathrm{H_2}$ is the hydrogen production.

The assumed value of $e_\mathrm{BOP}$ should be interpreted as an average value for an oversized offshore PEM electrolyser operating predominantly away from rated stack power.

## Model Limitations

This BOP model is intended for early-stage techno-economic assessment. It should not be interpreted as a detailed offshore BOP design.

The main limitations are:

| Limitation                                                                                | Implication                                                                                        |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Land-based NREL cost data are used as the cost basis                                      | Offshore packaging, redundancy, corrosion protection and maintainability are not explicitly costed |
| A generic {{< var bop-scaling-exponent >}} scaling exponent is used for the whole BOP | This captures broad economies of scale but not detailed equipment-train sizing |
| Water treatment scales with the aggregate BOP exponent | Package-size thresholds of water treatment are not represented |
| Offshore intake and installation costs remain unresolved | The quoted RO/deionisation package costs do not establish complete offshore water-system CAPEX |
| BOP electricity consumption is represented by a single average value                      | Dynamic behaviour, thermal transients and detailed part-load operation are not modelled            |
| Compression is excluded                                                                   | Any compression energy and cost must be added elsewhere in the model                               |

: Main limitations of the current BOP model.

The aggregate scaling approach covers the whole BOP, including water treatment. Offshore intake and installation costs and block-limit sensitivity remain explicit uncertainties.
